title: What the City’s auditors found about gift cards
question: What have the Controller’s auditors written about how departments buy, store and hand out gift cards?
finding: Three Controller audits since 2023 examined gift cards and each found controls that needed work. At the Human Services Agency ($2.8 million in under four years) the auditors found no site visits to the organizations handing cards out and one programme that used 1 of the 500 cards it was given. At Public Health ($487,060 over three years) 14 of 18 programmes reported not following at least one control, and 11 let one employee handle every step. At the Human Rights Commission $20,507 of cards was paid for with no approved policy and no proof of purchase. The reports record cards lost at two Public Health programmes and 25 cards handed to someone who was not a client; what all three have in common is records too thin to account for every card.
how: Passages copied word for word from three reports of the Controller’s City Services Auditor in the document library: the Human Services Agency audit of 1 February 2023, the Public Health audit of 29 February 2024 and the Human Rights Commission audit of 16 September 2025. Each quotation is checked against the text of the report by the script and is 25 words or fewer; the dollar figures are read from the same texts.
limits: An audit finding about controls is not a finding that money was taken. The Human Services audit runs into the first year of the pandemic, when some of the cards were emergency relief; Public Health’s programmes are small (its own limit is $50 a card); and the departments’ printed responses concur with the recommendations. The audits cover three departments and periods that ended in 2021 and 2024; no report on disk tests the others, or the nonprofits that buy cards with grant money. What would settle it: the Controller’s follow-up reports on whether each recommendation was carried out, and the inventory logs themselves.
